slides.title: Technical Implications
points: Security changes can affect connectivity, compatibility, availability, restarts, older applications, and dependent systems.
Objective 1.3 requires recognizing the technical consequences of a change before it reaches production.

slides.title: Allow Lists / Deny Lists
slides.teach: Allow lists define what is explicitly permitted; deny lists define what is explicitly blocked.

course.learn: Allow lists define what is explicitly permitted; deny lists define what is explicitly blocked.

breakdown.explanation: A change can require these lists to be updated so legitimate traffic is not blocked and unauthorized traffic is not accidentally permitted.
Firewall allow/deny rules, application allowlisting, email block lists, IP access lists.

course.why: Security changes often affect access-control rules. An incorrect list entry can break a service or unintentionally expose a resource.
course.example: A new application server cannot communicate with a database because its IP address was never added to the firewall allow list.
course.exam: Scenario clue: legitimate traffic is unexpectedly blocked or newly permitted after a change → ALLOW/DENY LISTS.
course.check_q: A new server cannot connect through a firewall because its address was not added to the permitted list. Which technical implication is most relevant?

slides.title: Restricted Activities
slides.teach: Restricted activities are actions that organizational policy, operational rules, or change controls prohibit under certain conditions.

course.learn: Restricted activities are actions that organizational policy, operational rules, or change controls prohibit under certain conditions.

breakdown.explanation: Some changes or activities are not allowed during particular times, environments, or business conditions.
Change freezes, no production changes during peak business periods, prohibited software installations, restricted administrative actions.

course.why: Restrictions protect critical operations and reduce the chance that high-risk activity occurs at the wrong time or without proper authorization.
course.example: During a holiday sales freeze, administrators are not allowed to make non-emergency production changes.
course.exam: Scenario clue: 'This action is not permitted right now or under this policy' → RESTRICTED ACTIVITIES.
course.check_q: A company prohibits non-emergency production changes during its busiest sales week. What does this represent?

slides.title: Downtime
slides.teach: Downtime is a period when a system or service is unavailable because of maintenance, failure, or a planned change.

course.learn: Downtime is a period when a system or service is unavailable because of maintenance, failure, or a planned change.

breakdown.explanation: Some changes temporarily take services offline, so the organization must understand and plan for the availability impact.
Planned outage, patching downtime, database migration outage, network maintenance interruption.

course.why: Downtime affects availability and business operations, so it should be evaluated, communicated, and scheduled appropriately.
course.example: A database upgrade requires the customer portal to be offline for 45 minutes.
course.exam: Scenario clue: service becomes temporarily unavailable during a change → DOWNTIME.
course.check_q: A planned upgrade makes an application unavailable for 30 minutes. Which technical implication is this?

slides.title: Service Restart
slides.teach: A service restart stops and starts an individual operating-system or application service so a change can take effect.

course.learn: A service restart stops and starts an individual operating-system or application service so a change can take effect.

breakdown.explanation: The whole system may stay online, but the specific service can be temporarily unavailable.
Restarting a web service, database service, authentication service, print service.

course.why: Restarting a service can interrupt users or systems that depend on that service, even when the underlying server remains running.
course.example: After changing a web-server configuration, the administrator must restart the web service before the new settings take effect.
course.exam: Scenario clue: one service must be restarted after a configuration change → SERVICE RESTART.
course.check_q: A configuration change requires restarting only the web service, not the entire application server. What is the technical implication?

slides.title: Application Restart
slides.teach: An application restart stops and starts an application so new code, configuration, or settings can be loaded.

course.learn: An application restart stops and starts an application so new code, configuration, or settings can be loaded.

breakdown.explanation: The application itself may need to restart, potentially interrupting users, sessions, or transactions.
Restarting an ERP application, restarting a web application, restarting a desktop application after an update.

course.why: Application restarts can affect availability and active user sessions, so they must be included in change planning.
course.example: After deploying a new configuration, the payroll application must restart and all active sessions will disconnect.
course.exam: Scenario clue: the application itself must restart and users may lose sessions → APPLICATION RESTART.
course.check_q: A configuration change requires the payroll application to restart, disconnecting active users. Which technical implication is this?

slides.title: Legacy Applications
slides.teach: Legacy applications are older systems that may depend on outdated operating systems, protocols, libraries, hardware, or security settings.

course.learn: Legacy applications are older systems that may depend on outdated operating systems, protocols, libraries, hardware, or security settings.

breakdown.explanation: A modern security change can break an older application that cannot support the new requirement.
Old software requiring TLS 1.0, applications that require deprecated libraries, unsupported operating systems, old authentication protocols.

course.why: Legacy compatibility is a major change risk because security hardening can disrupt applications that were built for older technology.
course.example: The security team disables TLS 1.0, but an old finance application stops working because it cannot use newer TLS versions.
course.exam: Scenario clue: an older application breaks after a modern security change → LEGACY APPLICATION.
course.check_q: After TLS 1.0 is disabled, an older application stops connecting because it does not support newer TLS versions. What is the main issue?

slides.title: Dependencies
slides.teach: Dependencies are systems, services, applications, libraries, or infrastructure components that another component relies on.

course.learn: Dependencies are systems, services, applications, libraries, or infrastructure components that another component relies on.

breakdown.explanation: Changing one thing can break something else that depends on it.
Database dependency, DNS dependency, authentication service, API, shared library, network route.

course.why: Dependencies create downstream risk. A change can succeed on the target system but still cause failures elsewhere.
course.example: A server change works correctly, but another application fails because both systems rely on the same authentication service.
course.exam: Scenario clue: another system breaks because it relies on the changed component → DEPENDENCIES.
course.check_q: A change to an authentication service causes several unrelated applications to fail. Which technical implication should have been evaluated?

hero.title: Technical implications
hero.intro: A change that is safe in isolation can still break connectivity, compatibility, availability, or a dependent system.

blocks.title: Technical implication scenario recognition
rows: Legitimate traffic unexpectedly blocked or permitted
Action prohibited during a defined period or condition
Service or system unavailable during change
One service must stop and start
Old software breaks after modern security change
Another system fails because it relies on the changed component

blocks.title: Identify what the change affected
items: Blocked or permitted traffic → Allow/Deny Lists
Access-control lists can accidentally block required traffic or permit something that should remain blocked.
Example: A new server cannot connect because its IP address is missing from a firewall allow list.
Not allowed right now → Restricted Activities
Policies or change freezes may prohibit certain actions during specific times or conditions.
Example: Non-emergency production changes are prohibited during a holiday sales freeze.
Unavailable → Downtime
If the system or service cannot be used during the change, the implication is downtime.
Example: A database migration takes the customer portal offline for 45 minutes.
One service reloads → Service Restart
A specific service may need to restart even though the whole server stays running.
Example: New web-server settings require restarting the web service.
The app reloads → Application Restart
The application itself restarts, which may disconnect users or interrupt sessions.
Example: A payroll application restart signs out all active users.
Old software breaks → Legacy Application
Older applications may not support modern protocols, libraries, or security controls.
Example: An old finance app fails after TLS 1.0 is disabled.
Something else breaks → Dependencies
If another system fails because it relies on the changed component, think dependencies.
Example: Several applications fail after a shared authentication service is modified.

questions.q: A new application server cannot reach a database because its address was never added to the firewall's permitted entries. Which technical implication is most relevant?
questions.explanation: The connection is blocked because the required system was not included in the allow list.

questions.q: A company prohibits non-emergency production changes during its busiest sales week. What does this represent?
questions.explanation: The organization has restricted certain activities during a defined period.

questions.q: A planned database upgrade makes the customer portal unavailable for 45 minutes. Which technical implication is this?
questions.explanation: Downtime is the period when the service is unavailable.

questions.q: A configuration change requires restarting only the web service so the new settings take effect. Which implication is most relevant?
questions.explanation: The individual service must be restarted.

questions.q: A payroll application must be restarted after deployment, disconnecting active user sessions. Which implication is most relevant?
questions.explanation: The application itself must restart, affecting active users.

questions.q: After TLS 1.0 is disabled, an older finance application can no longer connect because it does not support newer TLS versions. Which issue is this?
questions.explanation: The security improvement created a compatibility problem with an older application.

questions.q: A change to an authentication server causes several other applications to fail because they rely on that server. Which implication should have been evaluated?
questions.explanation: Those applications depend on the authentication server, so dependencies are the key concern.
